title: Schedule Risk Analysis for Long-Lead Transmission Equipment Procurement
content: Background: Most capital plans commit to a single date even though the arrival of a late transformer can delay energization of an entire transmission corridor. This study quantifies the schedule risk caused by long-lead transmission equipment, and compares the value for money of different procurement strategies. Method: A project-scheduling risk literature review and a supply chain risk literature review informed a structured synthesis, which in turn was used to develop a probabilistic model of a bulk-supply substation project, consisting of 23 activities and ten risks. A Monte Carlo simulation (20,000 trials for each scenario) was conducted to compare a baseline with four mitigation strategies: early award, a pooled strategic spare, dual sourcing, and a combination of the three. The comparison was facilitated by criticality indices, sensitivity analysis based on rank-correlation, and an expected-delay cost model. Results: The simulated mean energization date was 47.7 months, the eightieth percentile date was 51.0 months, and the probability of energization within 37 months was less than one percent. Half the slippage was due to the network structure and half due to discrete risk events. Award delay, transformer manufacturing time, factory congestion, and shipping delay were the most significant factors and the transformer chain was only critical in 56 percent of trials. Early award reduced the mean by 3.3 months, and produced the greatest net benefit assuming a delay cost. Conclusion: Confidence-based commitments, early award of critical equipment, and targeted protection give utilities more defensible long-lead procurement options. The case is illustrative, and the inputs are assumptions that can be adjusted using project data.
